item.text:
Below are the drafting and enforcement issues apparent from the supplied text. Constitutional vulnerabilities are potential challenges, not conclusions that a court would invalidate the bill.

### Definitions and coverage

1. **§ 2(1)—Coverage does not clearly follow derivatives or components.** The bill does not expressly cover copies, checkpoints, fine-tuned versions, distilled models, or systems assembled from covered models. Companies could argue that a downstream product is a different, noncovered system.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Single training run” permits splitting compute.** A developer could divide training among multiple runs, stages, models, or coordinated entities, keeping each below the threshold. The bill contains no aggregation rule.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Training compute excludes other capability-building methods.** The definition does not expressly count inference-time computation, search, scaffolding, tool use, or other post-training enhancements. Such systems would depend on a separate Secretary determination under § 2(1)(B).

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—The numerical boundary excludes exactly \(10^{26}\) operations.** “Greater than” leaves a run using exactly that quantity outside the compute-based definition. More broadly, a fixed threshold could become increasingly underinclusive as algorithms and hardware improve.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Compute measurement is unspecified.** The text does not establish how to count operations, handle numerical precision or sparsity, estimate unavailable measurements, or treat failed and repeated work. Companies could choose favorable accounting conventions, and prosecutors would lack a uniform standard.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Coverage may arise only after prohibited training has occurred.** A model apparently becomes covered only once it has been “trained using” more than the threshold. The bill does not clearly prohibit starting a planned above-threshold run or specify when ongoing training becomes unlawful.

7. **§ 2(1)(B)—“Secretary” is undefined.** The bill never identifies the official empowered to make capability determinations. References elsewhere to Commerce and the Secretary of State do not unambiguously resolve this.

8. **§ 2(1)(B)—The capability standard is materially vague.** “Substantially,” “human performance,” and “most cognitive tasks” lack benchmarks, comparison populations, and measurement rules. This creates inconsistent coverage and fair-notice concerns, especially with criminal penalties.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—The role of a determination is unclear.** The text does not say whether coverage begins upon an official determination or whether that determination recognizes preexisting coverage. The latter interpretation could expose earlier conduct to penalties without adequate notice.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—No determination process is specified.** There are no procedures for testing, obtaining evidence, notifying developers, issuing findings, updating determinations, or contesting them. Existing administrative law may supply some safeguards, but it does not supply the missing technical and operational framework.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—The Secretary’s discretion lacks detailed statutory constraints.** The bill delegates a consequential coverage decision without specifying assessment criteria beyond the broad capability phrase. That invites challenges concerning statutory authority, arbitrary decision-making, and potentially unconstitutional delegation.

12. **§ 2(1)—Key technical terms are undefined.** “Artificial intelligence model,” “artificial intelligence system,” and “training” have no statutory definitions. Developers could dispute whether unconventional architectures or particular capability-building activities qualify.

13. **§ 2(2)—“U.S. person” omits important categories.** The definition excludes lawful permanent residents abroad and does not expressly include partnerships, LLCs, trusts, unincorporated associations, or entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Some entity classifications may be contestable, creating avoidable gaps in overseas coverage.

14. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries are not expressly covered overseas.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary of a U.S. company is not itself a “U.S. person” under the definition. The bill does not expressly prohibit U.S. persons from directing, financing, or procuring covered activities through such subsidiaries.

15. **§ 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** Operators cannot reliably determine which processors count, and the registry could exclude alternative accelerators or other hardware capable of supporting covered training. There is no mechanism for updating the hardware criterion.

16. **§ 2(3)—The facility threshold can be avoided through distribution.** A company could spread chips among data centers or use facilities containing exactly 50,000 qualifying chips. There is no aggregation rule for connected facilities or commonly controlled infrastructure.

17. **§ 2(3)—“Data center” and facility boundaries are undefined.** Operators could dispute whether multiple buildings, leased suites, mobile installations, or distributed clusters constitute one facility. “Containing” also leaves unclear how installed, inactive, leased, and temporarily present chips count.

### Prohibition and exemptions

18. **§ 3(a)—The prohibited activities are insufficiently defined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” do not expressly address operating, accessing, distributing, selling, transferring, or releasing model weights. Some activities may fall within those verbs, but leaving that to interpretation creates enforcement risk.

19. **§ 3(a)—Supporting conduct is not expressly prohibited.** Financing, supplying compute, arranging offshore training, and assisting another entity are not independently addressed. General criminal aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy law may reach some conduct, but the bill supplies no comparable express civil rule.

20. **§ 3(a)—Domestic territorial coverage is unclear for remote activity.** “Any person in the United States” does not specify whether location refers to the actor, computing equipment, or prohibited conduct. Foreign operators providing covered systems to U.S. users could argue that their development and deployment occur abroad.

21. **§ 3(a)—Overseas enforcement mechanisms are missing.** The extraterritorial prohibition is express for U.S. persons, but the bill provides no tailored reporting, records, service-of-process, or overseas evidence provisions. Offshore operations could therefore remain difficult to detect and prove.

22. **§ 3(a)—No express interstate or foreign commerce nexus is required.** The prohibition reaches any covered conduct, including potentially wholly intrastate, noncommercial activity. Congress may have authority over much of this activity, but a jurisdictional element or developed legislative findings would reduce enumerated-powers challenges at the margins.

23. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering exempts systems, not merely completed training.** A covered system whose training began before enactment is exempt from all of subsection (a). On its face, the exception allows continued training, development, and deployment indefinitely, rather than merely protecting past conduct.

24. **§ 3(b)—A token pre-enactment start could secure permanent exemption.** “Training began” has no minimum-work, continuity, or completion requirement. A company could initiate numerous runs before enactment and claim exemptions for systems completed much later.

25. **§ 3(b)—The identity of a grandfathered system is undefined.** The bill does not determine whether later fine-tuning, retraining, architectural changes, mergers, or derivatives remain the same exempt system. Companies could characterize substantially new systems as continuations of old ones.

26. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering lacks verification requirements.** There is no registration, documentation, or evidentiary rule for claiming a pre-enactment training date. That makes disputed exemption claims harder to investigate and resolve.

27. **§ 3(c)—The safety-evaluation exemption is unrestricted.** Any actor could characterize otherwise prohibited training, development, or deployment as safety evaluation. The bill requires no authorization, independent supervision, security controls, compute limits, or restrictions on releasing resulting systems.

28. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities could qualify.** “For the purpose of safety evaluation” does not require an exclusive or predominant safety purpose. Commercial development containing a safety-testing component could claim the exception.

29. **§ 3(c)—There is no endpoint or disposition requirement.** The exception does not specify when evaluation must end or what happens to resulting models, weights, and checkpoints. It leaves room for indefinite exempt activity and disputes over subsequent retention or use.

### Registry and monitoring

30. **§ 4(a)—Registration has no deadline.** The bill does not say when existing facilities must register or when newly qualifying facilities must do so. Operators could argue that delayed registration does not violate a definite obligation.

31. **§ 4(a)—“Operator” and geographic scope are unclear.** The text does not allocate responsibility among owners, tenants, cloud providers, and managers, or specify whether foreign facilities operated by U.S. persons must register. Each ambiguity can leave relevant infrastructure outside practical oversight.

32. **§ 4(b)—Reporting applies only to registered operators.** An operator that fails to register can argue that the quarterly reporting obligation never attached. The provision should attach duties to operators required to register, not merely those who have registered.

33. **§ 4(b)—Report content and timing are inadequate.** “Describing the computing workloads” does not require customer identities, model identifiers, compute totals, training dates, or exemption claims, and no submission deadline is specified. A vague report could technically comply without enabling enforcement.

34. **§ 4(b)—Quarterly self-reporting offers weak detection.** A prohibited run could finish long before the next report, and operator certification is not backed by a specified audit or independent verification process. The bill requires neither advance notification of major runs nor prompt reporting of suspected violations.

35. **§§ 4–5—Registry violations have no express penalties.** Section 5 penalizes violations of § 3 only, leaving failure to register or report without a dedicated sanction. General false-statement law might address some knowingly false submissions, but not every omission or failure to comply.

36. **§ 4—No records-retention or customer-identification duties exist.** Operators need not preserve workload logs, compute accounting, or evidence identifying the responsible customer. Missing records could prevent proof of threshold crossing, attribution, or exemption eligibility.

### Enforcement and penalties

37. **§§ 3–5—No enforcement agency or procedural framework is designated.** Commerce receives registry information, but no provision expressly authorizes it to investigate § 3 violations or assess civil penalties. The bill leaves unresolved who brings civil cases, through what process, and with what administrative review.

38. **§§ 3–5—No tailored evidence-gathering authority is provided.** The text grants no express inspection, audit, subpoena, or compelled technical-testing powers. Existing governmental powers may help, but the bill supplies no complete mechanism for verifying private training activity or capability claims.

39. **§ 5—No express emergency or corrective remedies are supplied.** The bill does not authorize stop-work orders, injunctions, shutdowns, or disposition of unlawful models and checkpoints. Monetary and criminal penalties alone do not clearly ensure that a dangerous run or deployed system is promptly stopped.

40. **§ 5(a)—The unit of civil violation is unclear.** “For each day” does not specify whether separate models, runs, facilities, or deployments generate separate penalties, or when a continuing violation ends. This invites disputes over both penalty exposure and how violations are counted.

41. **§ 5(a)—The penalty ceiling may permit violations to become a business cost.** The bill includes no express disgorgement, revenue-linked penalty, or enhanced penalty for repeat violations. For sufficiently valuable projects, a capped daily civil penalty may provide inadequate deterrence.

42. **§ 5(a)—Civil liability lacks an express culpability standard.** The provision could impose liability without specifying knowledge, negligence, or reasonable reliance on an official determination. Combined with uncertain technical definitions, that increases fair-notice disputes and makes compliance harder to administer.

43. **§ 5(b)—“Willfully” leaves a consequential proof question unresolved.** Courts could differ over what knowledge of unlawfulness the government must establish. The bill should clarify the required mental state rather than leave prosecution of technically complex conduct dependent on that dispute.

44. **§§ 3, 5(b)—The prohibition may reach protected research or publication.** Undefined “develop” and “deploy” could be read to include publishing code, weights, or scientific work. Applications involving expressive activity could face First Amendment challenges, although not all AI development or deployment is protected speech.

### International agreement, duration, and commencement

45. **§ 6—The negotiating deadline is ambiguous and does not require an outcome.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” could refer to beginning efforts rather than completing negotiations. There are no milestones, reporting obligations, or consequences if no agreement results.

46. **§ 6—“Equivalent” international prohibitions could replicate domestic exemptions.** Because § 3 includes broad grandfathering and safety-evaluation exceptions, an agreement equivalent to that section could preserve the same escape routes. The provision also specifies no international verification or enforcement requirements.

47. **§ 7(a)—The safety finding lacks substantive criteria.** “Can be developed safely” does not specify acceptable risk, deployment conditions, or whether the finding must cover all covered systems rather than some subset. A narrow technical finding could be invoked to justify ending the entire prohibition.

48. **§ 7(a)—The National Academies report process is incomplete.** The bill does not commission the report, specify its scope, establish a schedule, or provide funding. “Acting on a report” also does not clearly require a favorable safety conclusion from the Academies.

49. **§ 7(a)—The legal mechanism for ending the prohibition should be explicit.** A joint resolution ordinarily requires presidential signature or a veto override to become law. The wording should require an enacted joint resolution, avoiding any suggestion that a congressional finding alone changes the prohibition.

50. **§ 7(b)—The unconditional sunset defeats the safety-based duration.** The entire Act expires after ten years whether or not safe development has been demonstrated. This removes the prohibition, registry, and enforcement provisions without requiring the § 7(a) finding.

51. **§ 7(b)—There is no express savings provision for existing violations.** Federal saving law may preserve accrued liabilities, but the bill does not expressly address pending investigations, proceedings, or continuing record obligations. Expiration could therefore generate avoidable disputes over enforcement continuity.

52. **§§ 5(a), 8—Penalty commencement conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 makes the Act effective 180 days later. The text should resolve whether any pre-effective-date conduct is punishable and avoid apparent retroactive liability.

53. **§§ 3(b), 8—The 180-day implementation gap permits additional development.** Companies can continue otherwise covered activities before the Act takes effect, although systems begun after enactment would not qualify for grandfathering. There are no interim preservation, notification, or anti-evasion obligations.

54. **§§ 2–8—Implementation authority and resources are missing.** The bill provides no express general rulemaking authority, implementation deadlines, or dedicated authorization of appropriations. Existing Commerce authority and funding cannot simply be assumed adequate for the new technical and enforcement responsibilities.

55. **Act generally—No severability clause addresses interconnected provisions.** A court could find provisions severable without such a clause, but the bill gives no express direction if a definition, exemption, or enforcement provision is invalidated. That leaves greater uncertainty about how much of the remaining prohibition survives.
